idiom_name: FXML markup + controller class with @FXML-injected fields and observable properties
implementation_notes: In JavaFX the declarative side is the FXML document and the container is the controller class: @FXML marks the fields and handler methods the loader may inject, so the controller owns the state and the scene-graph nodes stay passive displays driven by bindings such as textProperty().bind(model.countProperty().asString()). Prefer injection plus observable properties over runtime lookups - the controller then never needs to know node ids, and the FXML can be replaced without touching Java. Keep business logic in a model the controller wraps so the container can be tested with a stub.
pitfalls: In a named module the controller's package must be reflectively accessible - `opens <pkg> to javafx.fxml` - otherwise the loader fails with InaccessibleObjectException at runtime.
JavaFX is no longer part of the JDK: from Java 11 on it is a separate OpenJFX dependency, so a build that works locally can fail on a plain JDK.
Long-running work in a handler blocks the JavaFX application thread; move it to a Task and publish the result to the model.

variants.name: Swing: JPanel container coordinating passive child components
variants.idiom_name: JPanel subclass owning state; child components as passive displays
variants.implementation_notes: Swing's container story is explicit: a JPanel is a general-purpose container for lightweight components, and a JPanel subclass is the natural place to own state and coordinate the components it contains - the tutorial's ConversionPanel holds the model and wires its children exactly that way. Children stay passive: they display what they are told and fire listeners. Prefer this variant for existing Swing applications and desktop tooling; new Java UI work usually starts from the JavaFX variant.
pitfalls: Component mutations must happen on the event dispatch thread; call SwingUtilities.invokeLater from background threads or the component tree can end up inconsistent.
Child components that read the model themselves, or a model shared across windows, reintroduce the coupling the container removes.
Deeply nested panels with repeated revalidation make redraws expensive; keep the child hierarchy shallow and reuse components.
